facts.text: Robert FitzRoy, a naval officer already known as captain of HMS Beagle, founded and led the Met Office from 1854.
The new office was set up to study weather over the oceans in order to protect life and property at sea.
On the night of 25 October 1859 the Royal Charter gale destroyed 133 ships and killed about 800 people around Britain.
The Royal Charter, near the end of a two-month voyage from Melbourne to Liverpool, was driven onto rocks on Anglesey in Wales; about 460 people on board died.
FitzRoy argued that the storm could have been predicted and was allowed to test a storm warning service.
Coastal stations sent morning weather readings such as air pressure, wind and temperature to London by the new telegraph.
The first storm warning was issued in February 1861, shown by cones and drums raised on a mast.
On 1 August 1861 FitzRoy published the first public weather forecast in The Times.
FitzRoy’s forecasts contained errors and were heavily criticised by scientists who doubted forecasting was possible; he kept refining them.
FitzRoy died in 1865; a later government report recommended ending forecasting, and the last public forecast was issued in May 1866.
Storm warnings resumed in 1867 because of public demand, and public forecasts resumed in April 1879.
FitzRoy’s storm warning service survives as the Shipping Forecast, thought to be the longest-running national forecasting service in the world.
Today the Met Office runs its forecasts on supercomputers.
In 2022 the UN Secretary-General called for everyone on Earth to be protected by early warning systems by the end of 2027.
Only half of the world’s countries report having adequate multi-hazard early warning systems.
